name: Acetaminophen
mechanism: Analgesic and antipyretic acting centrally. The FDA label states the precise mechanism is not established, only that it is thought to be primarily central — it is not an anti-inflammatory and does not affect platelets.
labelIndications: Mild to moderate pain
Moderate to severe pain, alongside an opioid
Fever
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to acetaminophen
Severe hepatic impairment or severe active liver disease
interactions: Use with extreme caution in combination with any other acetaminophen-containing compounds
Alcohol enhances hepatotoxic effects
pearls: No effect on platelet aggregation or small-vessel hemostasis — the label is explicit, which is why it is the analgesic of choice when bleeding is a concern
Overdose is hepatotoxic; the ceiling matters more than the single dose
Antipyretics lower a fever driven by the hypothalamus. They do not treat environmental hyperthermia — cool the patient

Combination with other NSAIDs may cause increase adverse effects

name: Ketorolac
mechanism: NSAID with analgesic activity. The label describes the mechanism as not completely understood but probably prostaglandin synthetase inhibition, and notes it has no sedative or anxiolytic properties. Peak analgesic effect at 2–3 hours.
indications: Short-term (≤5 days) management of moderately severe acute pain requiring analgesia at the opioid level
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to ketorolac
Active peptic ulcer disease, recent GI bleeding or perforation — or any history of either
Asthma, urticaria or allergic-type reaction after aspirin or another NSAID
pearls: The label carries a Boxed Warning; the GI contraindication covers a past history, not just active bleeding, which is stricter than most NSAIDs
No sedation and no anxiolysis — an opioid-level analgesic that leaves the patient alert, which is its whole appeal
Prostaglandins hold the kidney’s afferent arterioles open; the same renal caution as ibuprofen applies

name: Aspirin
mechanism: The acetyl group binds a serine residue on COX-1, irreversibly inactivating the enzyme. Arachidonic acid can no longer become thromboxane A2, so the platelet cannot aggregate — for its whole 7–10 day lifespan.
indications: New onset chest pain suggestive of acute myocardial infarction (RI STP 3.02)
labelIndications: Chest pain suggestive of acute coronary syndrome
Reducing risk of death and MI in chronic coronary artery disease
Reducing risk of death and recurrent stroke after ischemic stroke or TIA
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to NSAIDs
The syndrome of asthma, rhinitis and nasal polyps — may cause severe urticaria, angioedema or bronchospasm
Active ulcer disease or active bleeding
Pediatric patients (Reye’s syndrome)

adverse.effects: bronchospasm, anaphylaxis, wheezing in allergic patients
GI bleeding, epigastric distress, nausea, vomiting, heartburn

interactions: Use with caution in patients allergic to NSAIDs
pearls: Irreversible is the point: the platelet has no nucleus and cannot make new COX-1, so effect lasts the platelet’s lifespan, not the drug’s half-life
The extended-release label carries a Limitation of Use — use immediate-release aspirin where rapid onset is needed, such as acute MI. Chewed, not swallowed whole
Aspirin-sensitive asthma travels with nasal polyps and rhinitis; ask about all three

name: Albuterol
mechanism: Beta-adrenergic agonist. Stimulates adenyl cyclase, raising cyclic AMP inside the cell, which relaxes bronchial smooth muscle. Preferential for beta-2 receptors, the predominant receptor in bronchial smooth muscle.
labelIndications: Relief of bronchospasm in reversible obstructive airway disease (asthma)
contraindications: History of hypersensitivity to any component

adverse.effects: headache, fatigue, lightheadedness, irritability, restlessness, aggressive behavior
pulmonary edema, hoarseness, nasal congestion, increased sputum

interactions: Tricyclic antidepressants may potentiate vasculature effects

doses: 2.5 mg via inhalation over 10-15 minutes. May repeat 3 times.
2.5 mg via inhalation over 10-15 minutes. May repeat 3 times.

pearls: Beta-2 selectivity is preferential, not absolute — the label notes 10–50% of receptors in the human heart are beta-2, which is why tachycardia, tremor and chest tightness follow a dose
Tachydysrhythmia and severe coronary disease are cautions to weigh, not label contraindications
Routinely combined with ipratropium; RI authorises both at AEMT

name: Terbutaline
mechanism: Beta-adrenergic agonist with a preferential effect on beta-2 receptors, relaxing bronchial smooth muscle. Given subcutaneously rather than inhaled, so it reaches a patient too tight to move air through a nebulizer.
indications: Bronchospasm unresponsive to nebulized interventions (COPD/asthma/RAD, etc.) (RI STP 2.08)
labelIndications: Prevention and reversal of bronchospasm in asthma, and reversible bronchospasm with bronchitis or emphysema, in patients 12 years and older

interactions: Cardiovascular effects exacerbated by other sympathomimetics
Beta blockers may antagonize terbutaline

doses: 0.25 mg IM (may repeat every 15 min x2)

Subcutaneous, not inhaled — the reason to reach for it is a patient moving too little air for a nebulizer to work

name: Ipratropium bromide
mechanism: Anticholinergic (parasympatholytic). Antagonises acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors on bronchial smooth muscle, preventing the rise in intracellular calcium that would otherwise constrict the airway. It blocks vagally-mediated reflex bronchoconstriction rather than stimulating relaxation.
labelIndications: Bronchospasm with COPD, including chronic bronchitis and emphysema (the labelled indication is maintenance)
Acute bronchospasm alongside a beta agonist — the prehospital use, authorised at AEMT by the national Scope of Practice Model and by RI

Hypersensitivity to atropine or any of its derivatives

adverse.effects: headache, dizziness, nervousness, fatigue, tremor, blurred vision
dry mouth, nausea, vomiting, GI distress

doses: 500mcg via inhalation over 10-15 minutes (may repeat x3)
500mcg via inhalation over 10-15 minutes (may repeat x3)

pearls: Different lever from albuterol: albuterol pushes the muscle to relax, ipratropium stops the signal telling it to squeeze — which is why they are given together rather than one instead of the other

The atropine cross-sensitivity is a contraindication in its own right, worth asking about

Fire risk: no smoking, no flammable material near a patient on oxygen
Secure cylinders upright. A falling tank that loses its valve becomes a projectile

name: Lidocaine
mechanism: Class IB antiarrhythmic. In Purkinje fibers it attenuates phase 4 diastolic depolarization and decreases automaticity, shortening action potential duration and the effective refractory period. It suppresses the irritable tissue without much effect on healthy myocardium.
indications: Cardiac arrest (pulseless V-tach, V-fib ONLY) (RI STP 3.03)
Pain relief during Intraosseous Access (RI STP 7.61)
labelIndications: Acute management of ventricular arrhythmias, such as those occurring with acute myocardial infarction or during cardiac manipulation
Prehospital protocol use (separate from cardiac SPL): Intraosseous (IO) analgesia prior to fluid infusion in conscious patients
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to amide-type local anesthetics
Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome
Stokes-Adams syndrome
Severe sinoatrial, atrioventricular or intraventricular block without an artificial pacemaker

adverse.effects: anxiety, drowsiness, confusion, seizures, slurred speech
hypotension, bradycardia, arrhythmias, cardiac arrest, AV Block

doses: 1-1.5 mg/kg slow IV/IO (may repeat x1 in 5min)
1 mg/kg rapid IV/IO (may repeat x1 in 10min)
1 mg/kg rapid IV/IO (may repeat x1 in 10min)

pearls: The WPW contraindication is on the federal label and was missing from this card entirely
Amide-type cross-sensitivity is the allergy question to ask — lidocaine, bupivacaine, ropivacaine all share it; the ester anesthetics do not
The IO-infusion-pain use is a different product label; this card is the cardiac arrhythmia label only

name: Procainamide
mechanism: Class IA antiarrhythmic. Lengthens the effective refractory period of the atria and, less so, the His-Purkinje system and ventricles, and slows conduction velocity. Its effect on the AV node is mixed — a direct slowing action set against a weaker vagolytic effect that can speed AV conduction.
indications: Documented, life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias such as sustained ventricular tachycardia
contraindications: Complete heart block — suppresses nodal and ventricular pacemakers, with a hazard of asystole
Known hypersensitivity to procainamide or procaine
pearls: Boxed Warning. The label restricts it to arrhythmias that are life-threatening in the physician’s judgement, explicitly because of proarrhythmic effects — the CAST trial showed excess mortality treating non-life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias
Complete heart block is hard to see behind a wide-complex tachycardia. If the rate slows during treatment with no AV conduction appearing, stop the drug
Long-term use is associated with a lupus-like syndrome and agranulocytosis — not a field concern, but it is why this drug fell out of favour

name: Metoprolol
mechanism: Beta-1 selective (cardioselective) adrenergic blocker, slowing rate and AV conduction. The label is explicit that the selectivity is not absolute — at higher plasma concentrations it also blocks beta-2 receptors in bronchial and vascular smooth muscle. No intrinsic sympathomimetic activity.
indications: Definite or suspected acute myocardial infarction in hemodynamically stable patients, to reduce cardiovascular mortality
Prehospital / RI Paramedic protocol use (off-label on IV SPL): Rate control in atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter with rapid ventricular response
contraindications: Heart rate < 45 beats/min
Second- or third-degree heart block without a functioning pacemaker
Significant first-degree heart block — PR interval ≥ 0.24 sec
Systolic blood pressure < 100 mmHg
Decompensated cardiac failure
Hypersensitivity to metoprolol or to another beta blocker — cross-sensitivity occurs
pearls: The thresholds are numeric and testable: HR < 45, SBP < 100, PR ≥ 0.24 sec. The PR cutoff was missing from this card
Cardioselective is relative, not absolute — enough drug reaches beta-2 to matter in a patient with reactive airways
Rate control in AFib or SVT is a common off-label use; this IV label covers acute MI only

name: Amiodarone
mechanism: Nominally a class III antiarrhythmic, but it carries electrophysiologic characteristics of all four Vaughan Williams classes — sodium channel block at rapid pacing frequencies, noncompetitive antisympathetic action, and prolongation of the cardiac action potential.

labelIndications: Initiation and prophylaxis of frequently recurring ventricular fibrillation and hemodynamically unstable ventricular tachycardia, in patients refractory to other therapy
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to any component, including iodine
Cardiogenic shock
Marked sinus bradycardia
Second- or third-degree AV block without a functioning pacemaker

adverse.effects: dizziness, fatigue, malaise, tremor, ataxia, lack of coordination
Adult respiratory distress syndrome, pulmonary edema, cough, progressive dyspnea
CHF, bradycardia, hypotension, worsening of arrhythmias, prolonged QT interval

interactions: Beta-blocker and calcium channel blockers may potentiate bradycardia, sinus arrest, and AV heart blocks
Concurrent use with procainamide not recommended without expert consultation

150 mg IV/IO over 10min (may repeat x1 if no response in 10min)

name: Diltiazem
mechanism: Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker. Inhibits calcium influx during depolarization in cardiac and vascular smooth muscle, slowing AV nodal conduction time and prolonging AV nodal refractoriness. Use-dependent — it works harder the faster the node is firing.
labelIndications: Temporary control of rapid ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter
Rapid conversion of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia to sinus rhythm
contraindications: Atrial fibrillation or flutter with an accessory bypass tract, such as WPW syndrome
Ventricular tachycardia
Sick sinus syndrome, or second- or third-degree AV block without a functioning ventricular pacemaker
Severe hypotension or cardiogenic shock
Concomitant administration with IV beta-blockers
Demonstrated hypersensitivity to the drug

adverse.effects: arrhythmias, CHF, peripheral edema, bradycardia, hypotension, AV blocks, syncope, V-fib, V-tach, cardiac arrest, chest pain

Second dose (if no response in 15min): 0.35 mg/kg IV/IO over 2 minutes (max dose: 25mg)

name: Nitroglycerin

Acute prophylaxis of angina pectoris

Soluble guanylate cyclase stimulators such as riociguat
Severe anemia — large doses can oxidize hemoglobin to methemoglobin
Hypotension or hypovolemia
Right ventricular infarction, where the ventricle is preload-dependent
interactions: Combination with other vasodilators or erectile dysfunction drugs can cause extreme hypotension

name: Activated charcoal
mechanism: A porous carbon matrix that adsorbs poison in the stomach, reducing absorption. It also works long after ingestion by interrupting enterohepatic and enterovascular recirculation of the poison (NLM PubChem, CID 5462310).

name: Hydroxocobalamin
mechanism: Cyanide binds cytochrome a3 and arrests cellular respiration, which is why a high dose kills within minutes. Hydroxocobalamin binds the cyanide ion to form cyanocobalamin — vitamin B12 — which the kidney excretes.

Label §5.5: the red colour interferes with colorimetric lab determinations — clinical chemistry, hematology, coagulation and urine parameters. Warn the receiving facility
Label §5.7: a blood cyanide level is not required to treat and must not delay treatment, though a pretreatment sample is useful for documentation

pearls: The label lists NO contraindications. Against a life-threatening nerve agent exposure there is nothing on the other side of the scale

Pralidoxime works best before the inhibited enzyme ages; delay costs effect, which is the argument for the auto-injector

Nursing mothers
Use as a local anesthetic

adverse.effects: drowsiness, sedation, seizures, dizziness, headache, blurred vision, paradoxical CNS excitement in children

interactions: Potentiates effects of alcohol and other anticholinergics
pearls: It competes with histamine rather than displacing it — which is why it cannot undo the histamine already bound, and why it is an adjunct to epinephrine in anaphylaxis, never a substitute
The neonate and premature-infant contraindication is absolute on the label, and extends to nursing mothers
The anticholinergic load is the side-effect profile: dry mouth, urinary retention, sedation, and delirium in the elderly

national.note: Anaphylaxis is an AEMT condition (Standards p. 41) but §V authorises only the epinephrine auto-injector.

RI 2.04P: 1 mg/kg (max 50 mg)

Treats rash and itch only: never replaces epinephrine

name: Thiamine (vitamin B1)
mechanism: Water-soluble vitamin B1. The body cannot store it long, and without it the enzymes of aerobic glucose metabolism stall — which is why a thiamine-deficient patient given glucose can decompensate.
indications: Patients with a history of alcohol abuse or who appear malnourished who are about to receive IV/IO dextrose (RI STP 2.10)
labelIndications: Hypoglycemia in patients with alcohol use or malnutrition
contraindications: History of sensitivity to thiamine or any ingredient
pearls: The partner drug to dextrose: the 50% dextrose label contraindicates use in alcohol withdrawal precisely because glucose without thiamine can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy
Labelled for thiamine deficiency and beriberi, dry (nervous system) or wet (cardiovascular)
Sensitivity is the only contraindication on the label; the WARNINGS section is where the rare anaphylactoid reaction to IV administration sits

national.note: Alcohol withdrawal is an AEMT condition (Standards p. 44); the drug appears in no national source.

Optional at AEMT, required stock at AEMT-C

name: Calcium chloride 10%
mechanism: Supplies ionic calcium, essential to the functional integrity of nerve and muscle and to myocardial contractility. In hyperkalemia it does not lower potassium — it raises the threshold potential back away from the resting potential, stabilising the membrane.
indications: Beta Blocker or Calcium channel Blocker overdose (RI STP 4.18)
labelIndications: Hypocalcemia, including hydrofluoric acid burns
Hyperkalemia — to stabilise the myocardium
Calcium channel blocker or beta blocker toxicity
contraindications: Cardiac resuscitation in the presence of ventricular fibrillation
Patients at risk of existing digitalis toxicity
Not recommended in asystole or electromechanical dissociation

adverse.effects: cardiac arrest, arrhythmia, bradycardia, hypotension, asystole, peripheral vasodilation

interactions: May antagonize the effects of calcium channel blockers
Do not mix or infuse immediately before or after sodium bicarbonate without intervening flush (forms salt crystals)

pharmacokinetics.duration: 20-30 minutes, but may persist for 4 hours (dose dependent)

pearls: The VF contraindication is specific and easy to miss: contraindicated for cardiac resuscitation while VF is present
Digitalis toxicity is the other hard stop — calcium worsens digoxin-induced arrhythmia
Sclerosing. Extravasation causes tissue necrosis and sloughing, so confirm the line and flush between this and sodium bicarbonate, which it precipitates with
Interchangeable with calcium gluconate per RI appendix 09.01; the gluconate is gentler on a peripheral vein

Interchangeable with calcium gluconate (service picks)
Incompatible with sodium bicarbonate

name: Nitrous oxide 50/50
mechanism: RI 7.41 states the exact mechanism is unknown. Its effects occur in the pain centres of the brain and spinal cord, thought to involve release of endogenous opioid peptides and serotonin activating descending inhibitory pathways, plus a GABA effect producing drowsiness. Onset 30–60 seconds, peak at 2–5 minutes.
labelIndications: Moderate to severe pain
contraindications: Altered mental status
Acute intoxication or drug use
Pregnancy, except during delivery
Blunt or penetrating chest trauma, or pneumothorax
Craniofacial injury, traumatic brain injury, or raised intracranial pressure
Undifferentiated abdominal pain
Diving emergencies — decompression illness
Respiratory distress
Maxillofacial abnormality, facial trauma or burns
Status post retinal surgery
interactions: Other CNS depressants potentiate CNS and respiratory effects
pearls: N2O diffuses out of blood INTO closed gas spaces — bowel, middle ear, pneumothorax — and expands them. That single property explains most of the contraindication list

Self-administered by the patient, so the patient must be able to understand and follow directions. The patient holds the mask, not the clinician — if they get too sedated the mask falls away, which is the built-in safety
Delivered as a 50/50 blend with oxygen in EMS, so it is never a hypoxic mixture
Among the few medications the national Scope of Practice Model names outright, at AEMT and Paramedic
